stories.summary: Dharmendra Pradhan has resigned as India's education minister following widespread protests by youth over exam paper leaks. event_overview.title: About Youth Protests
event_overview.subject: Youth Protests
event_overview.summary: Youth-led demonstrations in India grew around alleged irregularities in the 2026 National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test for undergraduate medical education (NEET-UG), including claims of a leaked paper and the disruption caused by a nationwide re-examination. The protests, centered visibly in New Delhi but supported more broadly, expanded into demands for accountability, examination-system reforms, and the education minister’s departure.

facts.label: Examination and re-test dates
facts.value: NTA scheduled NEET-UG 2026 for May 3, 2026; its official notices show that a re-examination was conducted on June 21, 2026.

facts.label: Examination purpose
facts.value: NEET-UG is the common, uniform entrance test for undergraduate medical education in India; it also applies to specified undergraduate Indian-system-of-medicine and homeopathy courses.

facts.label: Exam administrator
facts.value: The National Testing Agency (NTA), an autonomous organization under India’s Ministry of Education’s Department of Higher Education, administers NEET-UG and other national entrance examinations.

facts.label: Protest setting and stated demands
facts.value: The movement’s most visible sit-in site was Jantar Mantar in central New Delhi. Organizers sought the education minister’s resignation, examination reforms, and compensation for families of students reported to have died by suicide after exam irregularities.

facts.label: Legal context
facts.value: India’s Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024, in force from June 21, 2024, covers paper or answer-key leaks and related collusion among prohibited unfair means in covered public examinations.

explore_lenses.label: Which CJP demands were accepted?
explore_lenses.title: Resignation, case withdrawals and compensation
explore_lenses.summary: The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) said it ended its protest after talks with Union ministers produced commitments on its three core demands. The reported agreement also leaves broader examination-system reforms for later discussion.

claims.text: CJP spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka identified the group’s three central demands as Pradhan’s resignation, withdrawal of FIRs and other cases against protesters and organisers, and compensation for families of students who died by suicide following the NEET controversy.

After the talks, Ranka and fellow CJP spokesperson Saurav Das said the government had accepted the demands and called on protesters to leave peacefully; a federal minister likewise said the demands had been accepted.
CJP also submitted a five-point charter seeking wider education and examination reforms, which was described as subject to further consideration rather than completed implementation.

explore_lenses.label: Could Trump legally seek a third term?
explore_lenses.title: The Constitution bars a third election
explore_lenses.summary: Trump’s remarks were presented as jokes, but the Twenty-Second Amendment states that no person may be elected president more than twice. Changing that limit would require a constitutional amendment, not merely a campaign announcement.

claims.text: The National Archives’ text of the Twenty-Second Amendment says that no person may be elected to the presidency more than twice.

Article V requires a proposed constitutional amendment to receive approval from two-thirds of both houses of Congress, or a convention called by two-thirds of state legislatures, and ratification by three-fourths of the states.

Rep. Daniel Goldman’s H.Res.171, which was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in February 2025, states the view that the Twenty-Second Amendment applies to two terms in the aggregate and prohibits Trump from another presidential run; it is a resolution, not a constitutional amendment or binding court ruling.

explore_lenses.title: Madrid takes operational control across two areas
explore_lenses.summary: Spain's declaration is more than a warning label: it centralizes command for the affected parts of the Madrid region and Ávila. France, meanwhile, has sought European assistance to expand its firefighting capacity.

claims.text: Spain's interior minister declared an emergency of national interest on July 24 for the Madrid region and Ávila because of the concurrent fires, adverse weather, preventive evacuations, threats to population centers and the scale of resources required.

Under Spain's civil-protection law, the declaration places the interior minister in charge of ordering and coordinating state, regional and local resources; operational direction was assigned to the head of the Military Emergencies Unit.
France requested activation of the EU Civil Protection Mechanism for reinforcements, including Croatian Canadair aircraft, according to the French Interior Ministry.
The EU mechanism is designed to let countries request assistance when their disaster-response capacity is overwhelmed; it can coordinate offers of operational aid from participating states.

facts.value: In its UN notification, the United States said it was acting in cooperation with Israel, citing protection of U.S. forces and regional partners and the free flow of maritime commerce through the Strait of Hormuz. facts.value: The United States characterized its operations as necessary and proportionate self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter, including collective self-defense of Israel.

facts.label: Why the Strait of Hormuz matters
facts.value: The strait lies between Iran and Oman and links the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea. In the first half of 2025, about 20.9 million barrels per day of oil—roughly one-fifth of global petroleum-liquids consumption—moved through it, while alternative routes could replace only part of disrupted flows.

facts.value: The war affects territory across Ukraine, including areas near the frontline, cities far from it, and territory occupied by the Russian Federation; Kyiv is among the urban centres affected by long-range attacks.

facts.value: UN monitors reported that long-range weapons, including missiles and drones, were the leading cause of civilian casualties in June 2026, with many casualties occurring in urban areas far from the frontline; short-range drones were a major danger in frontline areas.

event_overview.summary: The event concerns a U.S.-Saudi agreement for peaceful nuclear cooperation, commonly called a “123 agreement,” signed on July 22, 2026 alongside a bilateral safeguards agreement. It establishes a legal framework for potential U.S. civil-nuclear exports and commercial participation in Saudi Arabia’s nuclear-energy program, while making nonproliferation, safety and security central stated objectives.

facts.label: Parties and date
facts.value: U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman signed the peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement and an accompanying bilateral safeguards agreement on July 22, 2026.

facts.label: Legal framework
facts.value: The accord is a Section 123 agreement under the U.S. Atomic Energy Act of 1954—the mechanism used for significant civil nuclear cooperation, including NRC-licensed exports of nuclear material, reactors, equipment and components.

facts.label: Congressional process
facts.value: The Department of Energy said the agreement would be transmitted to Congress for review; standard Section 123 agreements are subject to two review periods totaling 90 days of continuous congressional session before they may enter into force absent enacted disapproval.

facts.label: Stated purpose
facts.value: DOE describes the arrangement as supporting U.S. access to Saudi nuclear-energy opportunities and Saudi energy needs, while advancing nuclear safety, security and nonproliferation objectives.

facts.label: International safeguards context
facts.value: Saudi Arabia’s comprehensive safeguards agreement with the International Atomic Energy Agency has been in force since January 13, 2009; its Small Quantities Protocol was rescinded effective December 31, 2024.

event_overview.title: About Netanyahu Arrest Warrant
event_overview.subject: Netanyahu Arrest Warrant
event_overview.summary: The Netanyahu arrest-warrant event concerns an International Criminal Court (ICC) warrant issued for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the Court’s Situation in the State of Palestine. The warrant has become a focus of debate over the ICC’s jurisdiction, the alleged crimes identified by the Court, and whether national or local authorities can or must act if Netanyahu travels abroad.

facts.label: Warrant date and court
facts.value: ICC Pre-Trial Chamber I issued an arrest warrant for Benjamin Netanyahu on November 21, 2024, in the ICC’s Situation in the State of Palestine.

facts.label: Allegations at the warrant stage
facts.value: The Chamber found reasonable grounds to believe Netanyahu was responsible for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity, including starvation as a method of warfare, murder, persecution, and other inhumane acts. These are allegations supporting a warrant, not a conviction.

facts.label: Underlying investigation
facts.value: The ICC Prosecutor opened the Situation in Palestine investigation on March 3, 2021; it covers alleged Rome Statute crimes committed since June 13, 2014. The Court had held that its territorial jurisdiction for this situation extends to Gaza and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem.

facts.label: Jurisdiction dispute
facts.value: On November 21, 2024, the same ICC chamber rejected Israel’s then-pending jurisdiction and notification challenges, stating that Israel’s acceptance was not required for the Court to exercise territorial jurisdiction based on Palestine and that the jurisdiction challenge was premature at that stage.

facts.label: Enforcement framework
facts.value: The ICC does not itself carry out arrests; arrest powers rest with states. States Parties to the Rome Statute have obligations to cooperate with ICC arrest-and-surrender requests, while the United States is not a party to the Rome Statute.

event_overview.scope_note: This Muninn timeline follows New York City political and legal statements in July 2026 about possible action on the ICC warrant; it does not attempt to chronicle the full ICC case, the Gaza war, or all international responses to the warrant.

event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The Iran War refers to the 2026 international armed conflict centered on Iran, the United States and Israel, with effects extending across the Persian Gulf and neighboring states. U.S. combat operations began on February 28, 2026; the conflict has also made security and commercial navigation in the Strait of Hormuz a central issue.

facts.label: Start date
facts.value: The United States notified the UN Security Council that it commenced combat operations against Iran on February 28, 2026; U.S. energy officials likewise identify military action on that date as the point after which Hormuz traffic was effectively disrupted.

facts.label: Principal parties and stated U.S. purpos
facts.value: In its UN notification, the United States said it was acting in cooperation with Israel, citing protection of U.S. forces and regional partners and the free flow of maritime commerce through the Strait of Hormuz. These are the U.S. government's stated objectives, not an independent legal finding.

facts.label: Legal position asserted by the United St
facts.value: The United States characterized its operations as necessary and proportionate self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter, including collective self-defense of Israel.

facts.label: Why the Strait of Hormuz matters
facts.value: The strait lies between Iran and Oman and links the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea. In the first half of 2025, about 20.9 million barrels per day of oil—roughly one-fifth of global petroleum-liquids consumption—moved through it, while alternative routes could replace only part of disrupted flows.

explore_lenses.label: Can Congress force an end to the strikes?
explore_lenses.title: The House acted, but the next step is unsettled
explore_lenses.summary: On July 23, the House passed a measure directing the president to remove U.S. forces from hostilities with Iran. The immediate practical effect depends on Senate action and on how the administration responds.

claims.text: The House adopted H. Con. Res. 89 by 214-208 on July 23; its text directs the president, under section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution, to remove U.S. forces from hostilities with Iran.

Section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution says that when U.S. forces are in hostilities abroad without a declaration of war or specific statutory authorization, the president must remove them if Congress so directs by concurrent resolution.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal, who led the House resolution, argued that the war has no clear mission, strategy, or end goal; Trump has maintained that continued strikes do not amount to a return to war or a long-term operation.

As of the AP report published July 23, the Senate was expected to consider a similar resolution later that day; whether it passes, and whether the executive branch treats a resulting concurrent resolution as binding, was not resolved in the sources reviewed.

event_overview.title: About Tropical Storms
event_overview.subject: Tropical Storms
event_overview.summary: This tracked event concerns concurrent tropical cyclones affecting two U.S. National Hurricane Center monitoring areas: Bertha in the Atlantic basin, including the Gulf Coast, and Fausto in the eastern North Pacific. Tropical storms are named tropical cyclones with sustained winds of 39–73 mph; once sustained winds reach 74 mph, they are classified as hurricanes.

facts.label: Seasonal timing
facts.value: The Atlantic hurricane season, which includes the Gulf of America, officially runs from June 1 through November 30; the eastern Pacific season runs from May 15 through November 30.

facts.label: Geographic scope
facts.value: The eastern North Pacific basin is the portion of the North Pacific Ocean east of 140°W, while the Atlantic basin includes the Atlantic Ocean, Caribbean Sea, and Gulf of America.

facts.label: Storm classifications
facts.value: A tropical storm has maximum sustained winds of 39–73 mph; a hurricane has maximum sustained winds of at least 74 mph. Major hurricanes are Category 3–5 systems, beginning at 111 mph.

facts.label: Forecasting authority
facts.value: NOAA’s National Hurricane Center in Miami is responsible for tracking tropical cyclones in both the Atlantic and eastern North Pacific and issues operational products including forecasts, public advisories, discussions, and wind-probability information for active cyclones.

facts.label: Naming system
facts.value: Bertha is on the 2026 Atlantic storm-name list. Tropical-cyclone names are assigned from rotating lists maintained through the World Meteorological Organization system.

explore_lenses.label: Why does a Red Sea attack affect oil markets?
explore_lenses.title: It threatens an alternative Saudi export route
explore_lenses.summary: The concern is not only the damaged vessel: Saudi Red Sea terminals and pipelines have become more important alternatives when Persian Gulf shipping is constrained. Pressure on both routes reduces rerouting options and can raise transport, insurance, and supply-risk costs.

claims.text: EIA estimates that 20.9 million barrels per day moved through the Strait of Hormuz in the first half of 2025—about 20% of global petroleum-liquids consumption—while 4.2 million barrels per day transited Bab el-Mandeb.
Saudi Arabia and the UAE together have about 4.7 million barrels per day of pipeline capacity that can bypass Hormuz; Saudi Arabia's East-West crude pipeline can move oil to Red Sea terminals.
EIA reports that earlier Houthi attacks led some ships to sail around the Cape of Good Hope instead of using the Red Sea and Suez route, adding voyage time and cost.

AP reported that Saudi Arabia had recently exported about 4 million barrels per day through Yanbu on the Red Sea, making disruption near that route more consequential while Hormuz shipping is impaired.

explore_lenses.label: What would make this a lasting oil shock?
explore_lenses.title: Escalation and rerouting are the key tests
explore_lenses.summary: The next question is whether the incident remains a limited attack or deters shipping across the Red Sea. The Houthis describe the action as enforcement of their Saudi-linked shipping blockade, while Saudi and U.S. officials have called for the route to remain open or for de-escalation.

claims.text: The Houthis said they attacked two Saudi tankers, Encelia and Layla, because they allegedly violated the group's blockade; Saudi reporting and the UK Maritime Trade Operations center confirmed a fire on one tanker, but reporting on the second vessel was less independently confirmed.

The Houthis say their blockade responds to Saudi Arabia's blockade of Yemen and a recent attack on Sanaa's airport; Saudi Arabia's military says it will keep Bab el-Mandeb open, and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged the Houthis to stop.

Forecast: Goldman Sachs said Brent could exceed $120 per barrel in the fourth quarter and average $100 next year if Strait of Hormuz disruptions persist through 2027, with further upside if Bab el-Mandeb and the Suez Canal also face sustained disruption.

A sustained oil shock is therefore contingent on continued attacks, insurers and shipowners avoiding the route, and whether alternative pipelines and longer sea routes can move enough oil to offset the disrupted flows.

explore_lenses.label: Why is this Ebola outbreak unusually difficult to treat?
explore_lenses.title: The virus type lacks approved countermeasures
explore_lenses.summary: This is Bundibugyo virus disease, an Ebola disease for which no vaccine or treatment has been approved, unlike some outbreaks caused by Ebola-Zaire virus.

claims.text: Laboratory analysis confirmed Bundibugyo virus, and CDC says it is likely spread by direct contact with an infected person's body fluids; people are most infectious late in illness and after death.

WHO and CDC state that there were no approved Bundibugyo-virus-specific vaccines or therapeutics at the time of their updates; care therefore includes supportive measures such as fluids, electrolyte replacement, oxygen, blood-pressure management and pain control.

WHO, INRB, the University of Oxford and partners began enrolling patients in the PARTNERS randomized trial to test MBP134, remdesivir and their combination; these are investigational treatments, not established effective therapies.

event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The Iran War refers to the 2026 international armed conflict centered on Iran, the United States and Israel, with effects extending across the Persian Gulf and neighboring states. U.S. combat operations began on February 28, 2026; the conflict has also made security and commercial navigation in the Strait of Hormuz a central issue.

facts.label: Start date
facts.value: The United States notified the UN Security Council that it commenced combat operations against Iran on February 28, 2026; U.S. energy officials likewise identify military action on that date as the point after which Hormuz traffic was effectively disrupted.

facts.label: Principal parties and stated U.S. purpos
facts.value: In its UN notification, the United States said it was acting in cooperation with Israel, citing protection of U.S. forces and regional partners and the free flow of maritime commerce through the Strait of Hormuz. These are the U.S. government's stated objectives, not an independent legal finding.

facts.label: Legal position asserted by the United St
facts.value: The United States characterized its operations as necessary and proportionate self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter, including collective self-defense of Israel.

facts.label: Why the Strait of Hormuz matters
facts.value: The strait lies between Iran and Oman and links the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea. In the first half of 2025, about 20.9 million barrels per day of oil—roughly one-fifth of global petroleum-liquids consumption—moved through it, while alternative routes could replace only part of disrupted flows.

event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The Iran War refers to the 2026 international armed conflict centered on Iran, the United States and Israel, with effects extending across the Persian Gulf and neighboring states. U.S. combat operations began on February 28, 2026; the conflict has also made security and commercial navigation in the Strait of Hormuz a central issue.

facts.label: Start date
facts.value: The United States notified the UN Security Council that it commenced combat operations against Iran on February 28, 2026; U.S. energy officials likewise identify military action on that date as the point after which Hormuz traffic was effectively disrupted.

facts.label: Principal parties and stated U.S. purpos
facts.value: In its UN notification, the United States said it was acting in cooperation with Israel, citing protection of U.S. forces and regional partners and the free flow of maritime commerce through the Strait of Hormuz. These are the U.S. government's stated objectives, not an independent legal finding.

facts.label: Legal position asserted by the United St
facts.value: The United States characterized its operations as necessary and proportionate self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter, including collective self-defense of Israel.

facts.label: Why the Strait of Hormuz matters
facts.value: The strait lies between Iran and Oman and links the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea. In the first half of 2025, about 20.9 million barrels per day of oil—roughly one-fifth of global petroleum-liquids consumption—moved through it, while alternative routes could replace only part of disrupted flows.
